newsitem.title: PHILIPPINES: Financial openness mustn't hurt small fry - Malaysia.
newsitem.headline: Financial openness mustn't hurt small fry - Malaysia.

text.p: Pressure to make the world's financial markets more open must take into account fledgling economies and not leave them to the mercy of the big players, Malaysia's acting Prime Minister, Ibrahim Anwar, said on Tuesday.

"We should be supportive (of liberalisation)...but this has to be done in stages taking into account the legitimate concerns of developing economies," he told reporters in Manila where he spoke at a meeting of regional businessmen.
Issues have to be addressed such as how to protect smaller currencies from volatility, how to deal with speculative fund flows and ensure local financial institutions can survive a more open regime.
If these are looked at, then developing countries can take a positive role in talks within the World Trade Organisation, he added.
Earlier, WTO Director-General Renato Ruggiero told the business meeting that freer financial services were his organisation's priority to establish a strong global economy.

Commenting on the recent attack on the region's financial markets after the problems of the Thai baht, Anwar said it was crucial for a country's economic management to concentrate on long-term sustainability.
He cautioned against taking measures on the basis of popularity or based on the whims of speculators.
But exchange rates must be kept at realistic levels which reflected economic fundamentals though market sentiment may not be consistent with those fundamentals, he said.
"The authorities responsible for managing the exchange rates will have to be vigilant and must take necessary action to curb volatility," he said, urging gradual changes in currency rates.
Malaysia will continue to monitor the situation in Thailand closely, but in answer to one question Anwar said it was not true to say investors had lost confidence in the Malaysian stock market.
"This is temporary. They will come back. It is a matter of time," he said, dismissing concerns that Malaysia's property market was facing ruin.
